article_title: Are Students Dependent on AI in Writing Courses? Analyzing Factors Influencing Dependence on Generative AI Through the I-PACE Model
citation: Liu L, Zhuang M and Wang J (2026). Are students dependent on AI in writing courses? Analyzing factors influencing dependence on generative AI through the I-PACE model. Front. Psychol. 17:1905037. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1905037
title: I-PACE model extended to generative AI dependence in academic writing
description: The study applies the I-PACE (Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution) model, originally proposed to explain internet-use disorders, to college students' dependence on generative AI in academic writing. The Person component covers pre-existing individual traits such as academic self-efficacy and AI literacy; the Affect and Cognition components are represented by academic stress, perceived trust, and performance expectations; and the outcome is dependence. As the article states, "The 'Execution' component serves as the outcome variable, referring to the excessive reliance on generative AI, encompassing an individual'scognitivereliance,emotionalreliance,andtoolreliance on AI tools." The SEM results extend the model by showing a trust transmission mechanism from social influence to dependence.
requirements: Requires measurement of personal-trait, emotional-cognitive, and execution constructs in a specific technology-use context, as the study operationalized via adapted Likert scales
constraints: The article notes research on problematic AI-dependence behavior in educational generative-AI contexts is still in early stages
Tested in a cross-sectional, single-source Chinese undergraduate writing-course sample
target_learners: Chinese undergraduate students in academic writing courses
target_learning_goals: Responsible use of generative AI in academic writing and prevention of excessive AI dependence
examples: The study mapped academic self-efficacy and AI literacy to the Person component, academic stress, perceived trust and perceived usefulness to Affect/Cognition, and AI dependence to Execution, testing the paths with SEM on 229 responses
key_sources: Liu L, Zhuang M and Wang J (2026). Are students dependent on AI in writing courses? Analyzing factors influencing dependence on generative AI through the I-PACE model. Front. Psychol. 17:1905037. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1905037

article_title: Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math
citation: Theobald Elli J. et al. (2020). Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1916903117
title: Individual-participant-data meta-analysis datasets of examination scores and passing rates disaggregated by minoritized-group status
description: Two compiled datasets underpin the analysis: 9,238 individual student examination records from 15 studies and 51 course sections, and 44,606 student records on passing rates from 26 studies and 174 course sections, disaggregated by race/ethnicity/URM status or socioeconomic status (e.g., Pell Grant eligibility). The authors obtained raw by-student data by contacting authors of 297 eligible studies. All data are openly available: "All data used in the analyses are available at https://github.com/ejtheobald/Gaps_Metaanalysis".
requirements: Datasets must disaggregate student information by URM status or socioeconomic status to identify students from MGS
constraints: Only 41 of 297 coded studies provided disaggregated data usable for the MGS analysis
target_learners: Undergraduate STEM students across five to six disciplines, introductory and upper-division courses
target_learning_goals: Quantifying achievement gaps and instructional-treatment effects for underrepresented student subgroups
examples: The exam dataset came from five STEM disciplines and the passing-rate dataset from six, both including introductory and upper-level courses
key_sources: Theobald Elli J. et al. (2020). Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1916903117

article_title: A Breakthrough for Josh: How Use of an iPad Facilitated Reading Improvement
citation: McClanahan, B., Williams, K., Kennedy, E., & Tate, S. (2012). A Breakthrough for Josh: How Use of an iPad Facilitated Reading Improvement. TechTrends, 56(3). https://link.springer.com/journal/11528
title: iPad with reading apps and downloadable activities as the medium for individualized reading intervention
description: The iPad served as the presentation medium for a research-based tutoring plan for a struggling reader with ADHD. The tutor used applications such as FlashCards+, the Compound Boogie game, Stories2Go, Vocabulary Builder, Miss Spell's Class, ABC Alphabet Phonics, and an eBook with self-recording, plus downloaded graphic organizers and prediction guides. She reported that "the availability of applications and the ability to download Internet 'finds' directly to the iPad facilitated her planning and the implementation of the lessons." The device's touch screen, stylus notation, and audio recording enabled multimodal engagement with texts.
requirements: Applications and downloaded activities must be consistent with an approved, research-based plan of action
constraints: Some books the pair read were not available on the iPad, requiring a tape recorder for a similar recording effect; the tutor could not later recall the precise procedure used for on-screen INSERT marking
target_learners: Elementary struggling readers, particularly students with ADHD
examples: The tutor quickly created compound-word flashcards in FlashCards+ after the student asked to do the flash-card activity on the iPad instead of with paper cards.
key_sources: McClanahan, B., Williams, K., Kennedy, E., & Tate, S. (2012). A Breakthrough for Josh: How Use of an iPad Facilitated Reading Improvement. TechTrends, 56(3). https://link.springer.com/journal/11528

article_title: Word learning in deaf children with cochlear implants: effects of early auditory experience
citation: Derek M. Houston, Jessica Stewart, Aaron Moberly, George Hollich, and Richard T. Miyamoto. (2012). Word learning in deaf children with cochlear implants: effects of early auditory experience. Dev Sci. 2012 May ; 15(3): 448–461. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2012.01140.x
title: Modified Intermodal Preferential Looking Paradigm (IPLP) word-learning task with novel word/object pairings
description: The article describes a modified version of the IPLP word-learning task in which children are trained on two arbitrary novel-word/novel-object pairings (blick and modi) via video and then tested for preferential looking to the target. The authors state that the task 'more closely resembles real life word learning in that the words were arbitrarily related to the objects'. Performance is measured as mean longest look differences between target and nontarget during test blocks.
requirements: Requires children to sit and watch video stimuli in a sound booth; children who cried or were excessively fussy could not complete the procedure
constraints: Tested only at 12 or 18 months after initial CI stimulation; the version used may be a block or two longer than necessary, especially for older children
target_learners: 22- to 40-month-old deaf children with cochlear implants
target_learning_goals: Novel word learning (associating spoken nonwords with novel object referents)
examples: Children were presented with training movies where they could learn two novel-object/novel-word associations, then four blocks of test trials with reminder trials between blocks
key_sources: Derek M. Houston, Jessica Stewart, Aaron Moberly, George Hollich, and Richard T. Miyamoto. (2012). Word learning in deaf children with cochlear implants: effects of early auditory experience. Dev Sci. 2012 May ; 15(3): 448–461. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2012.01140.x

article_title: Participatory instructional redesign by students and teachers in secondary education: effects on perceptions of instruction
citation: Karin D. Könings, Saskia Brand-Gruwel, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2010). Participatory instructional redesign by students and teachers in secondary education: effects on perceptions of instruction. Instructional Science (2011) 39:737–762. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9152-3
title: IPSEE questionnaire measuring perceptions, desires, and their discrepancy across eight scales of a learning environment
description: The Inventory of Perceived Study Environment Extended (IPSEE) is a 56-item Dutch questionnaire measuring students' perceptions of a learning environment and their desires for its design, with each item answered twice on six-point scales. The "absolute difference between the scores on question A and B expresses the perceived-desired discrepancy", with small discrepancies indicating good fit. It has eight scales (fascinating contents, productive learning, integration, student autonomy, interaction, differentiation, clarity of goals, personalization); a parallel teacher version (IPSEE-T) has acceptable internal consistencies (alphas 0.68–0.87 for perception items).
requirements: Scales are sufficiently independent to warrant separate consideration, with no colinearity objections in the printed checks
constraints: Administered here only with 10th-grade pre-university students in Dutch secondary education
target_learning_goals: Measuring the degree to which characteristics of instruction are perceived present
Measuring fit between students' perceived and desired learning environment
examples: Each item pairs a statement such as 'All students do the same work at the same moment' with perception (A) and desire (B) questions
key_sources: Karin D. Könings, Saskia Brand-Gruwel, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2010). Participatory instructional redesign by students and teachers in secondary education: effects on perceptions of instruction. Instructional Science (2011) 39:737–762. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9152-3

article_title: Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Boetje, J., Sichterman, B., Van Ginkel, S., Smakman, M., & Versendaal, J. (2026). Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251338057
title: Design IPS learning tasks that reflect students' relevance perception, require integration of skills, knowledge, and attitudes, and simulate authentic real-life practice scenarios
description: Design principle 1 of the IPS-EDP model holds that IPS learning tasks should "reflect students' relevance perception (academic or professional)", require integrating skills, knowledge, and attitudes, and simulate authentic real-life scenarios to enhance IPS knowledge, skills, and performance. The review grounds this in the 4C/ID model's emphasis on authentic whole tasks and in empirical studies showing authentic assignments improve IPS performance and self-efficacy.
requirements: Tasks must align with students' academic or professional interests and require integration of knowledge, skills, and attitudes
constraints: Effectiveness of authentic tasks is primarily documented in long-term courses, suggesting these tasks require prolonged engagement
target_learning_goals: IPS knowledge, skills, performance, and self-efficacy
examples: Life science students in a problem-based learning course devising solutions for real-world drinking water problems showed increased IPS knowledge versus lecture peers; education students producing dyslexia brochures improved IPS performance
key_sources: Boetje, J., Sichterman, B., Van Ginkel, S., Smakman, M., & Versendaal, J. (2026). Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251338057

article_title: Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Boetje, J., Sichterman, B., Van Ginkel, S., Smakman, M., & Versendaal, J. (2026). Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251338057
title: Include multiple IPS instruction sessions in the curriculum and embed them within the content of the respective discipline
description: Design principle 2 recommends that designers "Include multiple IPS instruction sessions in the curriculum and embed these within the content of the respective discipline" to enhance IPS knowledge, skills, and performance. It draws on embedded librarianship and contextualization arguments, and is quantitatively supported by a meta-analysis showing extended semester-long sessions outperform one-shot instruction.
requirements: Instruction extended over time with increased contact frequency and integration within existing domain-specific course content
constraints: Short interventions (e.g., a one-day program) lacked lasting impacts on IPS self-efficacy; effects of a 15-hour embedded intervention did not persist on delayed post-test
target_learning_goals: IPS knowledge, skills, performance, and self-efficacy
examples: PICO training with weekly clinical reasoning sessions embedded in an evidence-based medicine course significantly enhanced IPS knowledge and self-assessed skills
key_sources: Boetje, J., Sichterman, B., Van Ginkel, S., Smakman, M., & Versendaal, J. (2026). article_title: Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Boetje, J., Sichterman, B., Van Ginkel, S., Smakman, M., & Versendaal, J. (2026). Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251338057
title: Provide opportunities for students to observe short fragments of peer-expert models interspersed with instructional guidance to increase IPS performance
description: Design principle 3 advises providing "opportunities for students to observe short fragments of peer-expert models, interspersed with instructional guidance, to increase IPS performance." It is theoretically grounded in social cognitive theory (observational learning reveals underlying cognitive processes and strengthens self-efficacy) and cognitive load theory (modeling examples reduce cognitive load and support schema construction).
requirements: Model fragments should be short, show each IPS process step, be interspersed with reflective prompts or explicit instruction, and be followed by practice
constraints: Evidence for non-expert (peer) models is mixed and based on varied operationalizations with unvalidated outcome measures
examples: Peer-expert videos showing short fragments of each IPS process step, interspersed with reflective prompts or explicit instruction and followed by practice, outperformed practice-only groups on IPS performance

article_title: Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Boetje, J., Sichterman, B., Van Ginkel, S., Smakman, M., & Versendaal, J. (2026). Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251338057
title: Provide opportunities for students to practice IPS in preparation for or following instruction or modeling
description: Design principle 4 states: "Provide opportunities for students to practice IPS in preparation for or following instruction or modeling to develop IPS knowledge, skills, and performance." Fifty-three of the reviewed publications adopted practice as a crucial learning environment characteristic, and theoretical arguments drew on social constructivist theory, collaborative practice principles, and the 4C/ID model's emphasis on part-task practice and repetition.
requirements: Practice should be scheduled in preparation for or following instruction or modeling; the literature suggests combining deliberate practice with instruction or modeling examples to enhance skill retention and knowledge acquisition
examples: Fifty-three of the reviewed publications adopted the opportunity to practice IPS as a crucial learning environment characteristic to improve IPS knowledge, skills, and performance

article_title: Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Boetje, J., Sichterman, B., Van Ginkel, S., Smakman, M., & Versendaal, J. (2026). Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251338057
title: IPS-EDP model: seven educational design principles for developing information problem solving competence organized by constructive alignment
description: The IPS educational design principles (IPS-EDP) model integrates seven design principles—"encompassing (1) learning task, (2) instruction, (3) modeling, (4) practice, (5) learning activities, (6) support, and (7) feedback"—derived from a systematic review of 69 peer-reviewed articles. Sequenced according to Biggs's constructive alignment, the principles move from intended learning outcomes (principle 1) through teaching and learning activities (principles 2–6) to assessment strategies (principle 7), providing a theoretical foundation for designing IPS learning environments in higher education.
requirements: It is recommended to apply at least one principle from each component of constructive alignment within the learning environment; comprehensive application of each principle is not imperative
constraints: Empirical evidence predominantly addressed information search and selection, potentially limiting generalizability to broader IPS competence
target_learning_goals: IPS competence: knowledge, skills, attitudes, performance, and self-efficacy
examples: The model summarizes how the seven principles address learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities, and assessment strategies, mirroring the stages of course development

Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251338057

article_title: Observational, student, and teacher perspectives on interpersonal teacher behavior: Shared and unique associations with teacher and student emotions
citation: Donker, M. H., van Vemde, L., Hessen, D. J., van Gog, T., & Mainhard, T. (2021). Observational, student, and teacher perspectives on interpersonal teacher behavior: Shared and unique associations with teacher and student emotions. Learning and Instruction, vol. 73, 101414. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101414
title: Interpersonal theory and the Interpersonal Circle for Teachers (IPC-T): Agency and Communion as two sufficient dimensions of interpersonal teacher behavior
description: Interpersonal theory is the framework the article uses to operationalize teachers' interpersonal behavior in class. It "postulates that to describe behavior of people in interaction with others two dimensions are at the same time needed and sufficient", denoted by the meta-labels Agency (taking the lead, social influence, control) and Communion (friendliness, affection, warmth). Wubbels, Créton, and Hooymayers adapted this theory to the classroom setting as the Interpersonal Circle for Teachers (IPC-T), in which all prototypical teacher behaviors around the circle are specific combinations of agency and communion, such as being hesitant (low agency) or imposing (high agency, moderately low communion).
requirements: Both dimensions are needed at the same time to describe interpersonal behavior; all teacher behaviors are characterized as a specific combination of agency and communion
target_learning_goals: understanding interpersonal teacher behavior as antecedent of teacher and student emotions
examples: The article illustrates combinations: a teacher can be hesitant to act (uncertain; moderately low communion and low agency) or employ strict classroom management (imposing; moderately low communion and high agency)
key_sources: Donker, M. H., van Vemde, L., Hessen, D. J., van Gog, T., & Mainhard, T. (2021). Observational, student, and teacher perspectives on interpersonal teacher behavior: Shared and unique associations with teacher and student emotions. Learning and Instruction, vol. 73, 101414. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101414

article_title: Cerebellar interpositus nucleus exhibits time-dependent errors and predictive responses
citation: Parras, G. G., Delgado-García, J. M., López-Ramos, J. C., Gruart, A., & Leal-Campanario, R. (2024). Cerebellar interpositus nucleus exhibits time-dependent errors and predictive responses. npj Science of Learning 9, 12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00224-y
title: The cerebellar IPn operates as an active-inference (Bayesian) system that minimizes prediction errors across learning stages
description: The article proposes that the IPn functions as an active inference system linking action and perception, operating by "comparing predicted states with actual states, learning from errors, and updating its internal representations" to minimize future errors. Its firing pattern is learning-stage-dependent: long-lasting error responses before acquisition, reduced errors midway, and predictive (conditioned) responses once learning is established. The discussion states that "the ﬁring pattern of IPn neurons matches the Bayesian inference, where the response to current stimuli is based on the likelihood of the previous experience", so the IPn generates predictions of the upcoming US.
requirements: A hierarchical organization is stated as fundamental for correct inference, with CS and US information converging at the cerebellar cortex and IPn via mossy and climbing fibers
constraints: The framework is advanced here for a delay classical eyeblink conditioning paradigm in rabbits using an auditory CS; the authors note cerebellum-dependent learning and timing are more complex than previously thought
target_learners: Adult male rabbits undergoing classical eyeblink conditioning
target_learning_goals: Acquisition and timing refinement of a conditioned eyelid (motor) response through error minimization
key_sources: Parras, G. G., Delgado-García, J. M., López-Ramos, J. C., Gruart, A., & Leal-Campanario, R. (2024). Cerebellar interpositus nucleus exhibits time-dependent errors and predictive responses. npj Science of Learning 9, 12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00224-y

article_title: Common learning activities, teaching strategies, and facilitation practices in interprofessional education-a scoping review.
citation: Chan Alice Mei Ling, Yip Agnes Wing Ki, Cheung Jasmine, Wong Julia Sze Wing, Cheng James Tse Wai, Chan Shun, Kwan Rick Yiu Cho. (2026). Common learning activities, teaching strategies, and facilitation practices in interprofessional education—a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09255-y
title: Four-category taxonomy of IPE learning activities: small-group, simulation, theoretical, and clinical
description: The review organizes IPE learning activities into a taxonomy of nine types under four categories. It states that "Nine types of learning activities were identified under four learning categories: (1) small-group; (2) simulation; (3) theoretical, and (4) clinical". Small-group covers case-based and problem-based discussion; simulation covers mannequin, virtual, standardized-patient, and role-play formats; theoretical covers modules and presentations; clinical covers supervised hands-on practice. The taxonomy was derived thematically from the 41 included studies and is intended to inform design of future IPE interventions.
requirements: Activities must involve two or more healthcare disciplines collaborating with active interactions, per the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: Derived from studies published 2014–2024 in English; the review did not evaluate the effectiveness of the activity types
target_learners: undergraduate healthcare students in medicine, nursing, and allied health
examples: The review's Table 2 defines each activity type, e.g., case-based discussion as students discussing real or hypothetical cases to develop higher-order thinking
key_sources: Chan Alice Mei Ling, Yip Agnes Wing Ki, Cheung Jasmine, Wong Julia Sze Wing, Cheng James Tse Wai, Chan Shun, Kwan Rick Yiu Cho. (2026). Common learning activities, teaching strategies, and facilitation practices in interprofessional education—a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09255-y

article_title: Common learning activities, teaching strategies, and facilitation practices in interprofessional education-a scoping review.
citation: Chan Alice Mei Ling, Yip Agnes Wing Ki, Cheung Jasmine, Wong Julia Sze Wing, Cheng James Tse Wai, Chan Shun, Kwan Rick Yiu Cho. (2026). Common learning activities, teaching strategies, and facilitation practices in interprofessional education—a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09255-y
title: Design IPE sessions around a clear topic, shared pre-reading, and explicit review of each profession's roles to reduce role ambiguity
description: The review's synthesis of teaching strategies supports preparing learners before collaborative activity. It reports that offering pre-reading materials establishes a shared foundation of knowledge and "may diminish perceptions of ambiguity in interprofessional training", while briefing sessions or printed materials on roles and responsibilities "established a foundation of mutual respect to enhance work efficiency and resolve interprofessional conflicts". Establishing a clear topic provides direction ensuring learners achieve desired outcomes and helps them recognize the importance of teamwork.
requirements: Pre-reading materials must be distributed ahead of sessions; role briefings should occur before interprofessional training begins
constraints: Drawn from studies of undergraduate healthcare students in IPE settings; the review did not test strategy effectiveness
target_learners: undergraduate healthcare students from two or more professions
target_learning_goals: role clarity, interprofessional respect, and teamwork
examples: Clarke et al. structured a 1.5-hour discussion session with mandatory pre-class reading assigned 2 weeks before training; Gill et al. prepared a comprehensive introduction to interprofessional teamwork theory delivered prior to placements

article_title: Competencies and pedagogical foundations for faculty development in interprofessional health education: a scoping review.
citation: Leite Daniella Rosaly; Carneiro Patrícia Silva; Mininel Vivian Aline; Rossit Rosana Aparecida Salvador; Leonello Valéria Marli; Gonçalves Geisa Colebrusco de Souza; da Silva Jaqueline Alcântara Marcelino. (2025). Competencies and pedagogical foundations for faculty development in interprofessional health education: a scoping review. Revista da Escola de Enfermagem da USP. https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-220X-REEUSP-2024-0421en
title: Two-category taxonomy of faculty development competencies for interprofessional health education: collaborative/facilitation competencies and pedagogical foundations
description: This scoping review proposes a two-category taxonomy for faculty development competencies in interprofessional health education. The first category covers interprofessional collaborative and facilitation competencies for IPE, drawing on the CIHC and IPEC frameworks. The second category covers pedagogical, theoretical, and methodological foundations including learning theories, teaching-learning strategies, and assessment processes. The review concludes that "the domains of competencies for faculty development in IPE can be divided into two groups: 1) Interprofessional collaborative and facilitation competencies for IPE and 2) Pedagogical, theoretical, and methodological foundations for faculty development in IPE."
requirements: Faculty development initiatives in IPE should address both interprofessional collaborative competencies and pedagogical foundations
constraints: The review notes that user-, family-, and community-centered care remains incipient in the analyzed studies despite being present in the analytical frameworks

article_title: A scoping review of interprofessional education in healthcare: evaluating competency development, educational outcomes and challenges.
citation: Patel Hemal, Perry Simone, Badu Eric, Mwangi Felista, Onifade Oyepeju, Mazurskyy Alexander, Walters Joanne, Tavener Meredith, Noble Danielle, Chidarikire Sherphard, Lethbridge Lee, Jobson Liam, Carver Hamish, MacLellan Annabelle, Govind Natalie, Andrews Graham, Kerrison-Watkin Greg, Lun Elizabeth, Malau-Aduli Bunmi S. (2025). A scoping review of interprofessional education in healthcare: evaluating competency development, educational outcomes and challenges. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06969-3
title: IPEC framework of four core competencies for interprofessional collaboration
description: The Interprofessional Education Collaborative (IPEC) framework identifies "four core competencies of interprofessional collaboration": Values and Ethics, Roles and Responsibilities, Communication, and Teams and Teamwork. The review states these competencies "enhance patient care, promote population health and reduce healthcare costs". The review used this framework deductively, mapping inductively derived themes and sub-themes from 88 included studies onto the four IPEC competencies to determine which competencies IPE develops.
requirements: Studies must report on IPE activities involving two or more professions working collaboratively in healthcare settings for mapping to the framework to be applicable
constraints: The review notes the extent to which IPE sessions foster acquisition of these competencies had not previously been investigated
target_learners: undergraduate healthcare students (medicine, nursing, pharmacy, allied health)
target_learning_goals: interprofessional collaborative practice competencies: teamwork, communication, roles and responsibilities, values and ethics
examples: The review mapped 88 studies' competency outcomes onto the four IPEC competencies, finding Teams and Teamwork most frequently developed (65 instances)

article_title: A scoping review of interprofessional education in healthcare: evaluating competency development, educational outcomes and challenges.
citation: Patel Hemal, Perry Simone, Badu Eric, Mwangi Felista, Onifade Oyepeju, Mazurskyy Alexander, Walters Joanne, Tavener Meredith, Noble Danielle, Chidarikire Sherphard, Lethbridge Lee, Jobson Liam, Carver Hamish, MacLellan Annabelle, Govind Natalie, Andrews Graham, Kerrison-Watkin Greg, Lun Elizabeth, Malau-Aduli Bunmi S. (2025). A scoping review of interprofessional education in healthcare: evaluating competency development, educational outcomes and challenges. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06969-3
title: Two-theme structure of IPE competency development: personal professional growth and professional interactional skills
description: Inductive content analysis of the included articles identified "two themes and eight sub-themes explaining the core competencies developed by healthcare students during their IPE learning experiences". The two themes are "personal professional growth and professional interactional skills/ competencies". Personal professional growth covers collaborative learning, professional identity and confidence building, role clarity, and effective communication, while professional interactional skills covers shared person-centred care, collaborative work, support and supervision, and equality and respect.
requirements: IPE activities must occur in clinical practice settings with two or more professions for this thematic structure to apply
constraints: The review excluded studies describing programs without any students' outcome measured and settings without experiential learning
examples: The eight sub-themes include collaborative learning, professional identity and confidence building, role clarity, effective communication, shared person-centred care, collaborative work, support and supervision, and equality and respect

article_title: Third Graders' Understanding of Air Concepts Facilitated by the iPod Inquiry Teaching Method
citation: Lai, C. (2016). Third graders' understanding of air concepts facilitated by the iPod inquiry teaching method. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(1), 1-9. https://www.ijres.net
title: iPod inquiry teaching method
description: The iPod inquiry teaching method is a constructivist science inquiry sequence integrating the POE strategy with the STS strategy. As the article states, Lai (2009) proposed "a format for scientific inquiry teaching with the features of 'invitation- Prediction- operation- discussion (referred to as iPod inquiry teaching)'". It retains POE's prediction step, converts observation into hands-on operation, and converts explanation into peer discussion, aiming to give students space to construct their own ideas and understand a concept framework. In this study it structured the experimental group's teaching of the air concept unit.
requirements: Teachers retain the prediction step to expose students' prior misconceptions and avoid over-guiding during invitation
Students record findings during hands-on operations and every student shares ideas in the discussion step
constraints: Evaluated here only for a third-grade air concept unit in Taiwanese primary schools with equal teaching hours across groups
examples: The experimental group's teaching integrated the Invitation, Prediction, Operation, and Discussion steps into the procedures for the 'Invisible Air' unit
key_sources: Lai, C. (2016). Third graders' understanding of air concepts facilitated by the iPod inquiry teaching method. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(1), 1-9. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105183

article_title: Third Graders' Understanding of Air Concepts Facilitated by the iPod Inquiry Teaching Method
citation: Lai, C. (2016). Third graders' understanding of air concepts facilitated by the iPod inquiry teaching method. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(1), 1-9. https://www.ijres.net
title: Four features of iPod inquiry teaching: involvement, prediction, operation, discussion
description: The article summarizes iPod inquiry teaching's focus and features as four points: positive and diverse teaching activities that encourage student involvement and trigger motives; retaining the prediction step from POE to fully understand students' misconceptions of prior concepts; changing the observation step into an operation step so students participate actively through hands-on activities; and changing the explanation step into a discussion step that connects scientific phenomena and theories through group discussion. The pattern operates at lesson level within a science unit.
requirements: Lively learning situations that trigger student interest
Teachers identify misconceptions during prediction and revise or complement students' knowledge
constraints: Described by the author from prior work (Lai, 2009) rather than independently validated in this study
examples: In the study, multimedia video animations, science toys and modeling balloons were used in the invitation step, followed by prediction, hands-on operations, and peer discussion

title: Author-designed educational games built with three iPad applications (TINY TAP, Quiz Maker, Puzzle Maker) plus a teacher guidebook
description: The author designed educational games using iPad applications specialized for designing games in templates, permitting adding cognitive content, images and maps for the (Resources of my Country) unit. The study comprises three applications: "TINY TAP", "Quiz Maker" and "Puzzle Maker". Games were reviewed by specialists and experienced teachers, piloted in another school, and applied by the class teacher with four iPads shared among four student groups.
requirements: Games were designed following preparation, design, and production/development stages including task, learners' and content analysis
A teacher guidebook explaining the teaching method was provided
constraints: Only four iPads were available; Quiz maker lacks a sharing option so questions were created on one device connected to a data show
target_learning_goals: social studies knowledge and concepts of the Resources of my Country unit
examples: Students of the experimental class were divided into four groups and provided four iPads used during the lesson at the teacher's request

title: Eight design standards for educational games-based iPad applications
description: Adopting standards the article attributes to Attia (2008) as effective programming standards, the author lists criteria for preparing educational games-based iPad applications so they achieve their educational objectives. These include designing "according to the objectives that the learner will achieve after learning", including instructions and guidelines showing playing method, providing participation and positive interaction, involving attraction and entertainment, being easily used so the learner will not feel disappointed, involving feedback and enhancement, considering principles of learning, and involving audio, video, images and illustrations.
requirements: They should involve instructions and guidelines that show playing method, especially if the game is based on self-learning
They involve feedback and enhancement
target_learners: primary school students using iPad games
target_learning_goals: achievement of unit learning objectives through game-based activities
examples: The author applied these standards when designing the TINY TAP, Puzzle Maker and Quiz Maker games for the Resources of my Country unit

article_title: iPadegogy of Reading: Do iPads Influence Student's Reading?
citation: Roser, M. (2017). iPadegogy of reading: Do iPads influence studens' reading? Teachers and Curriculum, 17(2), 25-32. http://dx.doi.org/10.15663/tandc.v17i2.176
title: View iPads as a teaching and learning tool whose effectiveness depends on the teacher, not as a direct driver of achievement
description: The article argues against a narrow, deterministic view of iPads: they should be viewed as a teaching and learning tool offering e-reader supports (dictation, dictionary, adjustable fonts) and affordances for engagement and collaborative learning. Because the study found minimal direct influence on reading achievement, the article holds that "it is themselves at the head and the heart of the classroom which ultimately dictates the effectiveness of the iPad as a tool".
requirements: Educators and institutions must comprehend that the teacher, not the device, dictates the iPad's classroom effectiveness
constraints: The study found iPads had minimal direct influence on reading achievement, so the device cannot be assumed to be a panacea for reading achievement issues
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension, accuracy and rate; reading engagement
examples: In the five-week study, the treatment group read a novel as an e-book and completed supporting activities with iPad applications while the control group used a soft-bound copy and pen-and-paper bookwork

article_title: Student and Instructor Perceptions of the Usefulness of Computer-Based Microworlds in Supporting the Teaching and Assessment of Computer Networking Skills: An Exploratory Study
citation: Dabbagh, N., & Beattie, M. (2010). Student and Instructor Perceptions of the Usefulness of Computer-Based Microworlds in Supporting the Teaching and Assessment of Computer Networking Skills: An Exploratory Study. Advances in Engineering Education. https://www.aee.org
title: Internet Protocol Learning Microworld (IPLM)
description: The IPLM is a computer-based microworld that simulates complex computer network environments, allowing students to experiment with hardware (ethernet) connection changes and internet protocol (IP) configurations. It includes a main configuration screen, two diagnostic screens, simulated network services (DNS, web server, DHCP, routing), and a set of six increasingly complex problem-solving tasks with difficulty point scores from 1 to 5. Students build networks from simple to complex configurations using drag-and-drop icons and simulated cables.
requirements: Designed for students enrolled in networking classes with some prior networking knowledge
constraints: Focuses on configuration and troubleshooting of a single layer (layer 3) of the OSI model
examples: Students dragged icons representing computers, switches, and modems, connected them with simulated cables, configured IP assignments, and tested communication using a simulated web browser and command shell
key_sources: Dabbagh, N., & Beattie, M. (2010). Student and Instructor Perceptions of the Usefulness of Computer-Based Microworlds in Supporting the Teaching and Assessment of Computer Networking Skills: An Exploratory Study. Advances in Engineering Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1076143

article_title: Student and Instructor Perceptions of the Usefulness of Computer-Based Microworlds in Supporting the Teaching and Assessment of Computer Networking Skills: An Exploratory Study
citation: Dabbagh, N., & Beattie, M. (2010). Student and Instructor Perceptions of the Usefulness of Computer-Based Microworlds in Supporting the Teaching and Assessment of Computer Networking Skills: An Exploratory Study. Advances in Engineering Education. https://www.aee.org
title: Internet Protocol Assessment Microworld (IPAM)
description: The IPAM is largely identical to the IPLM but incorporates minor changes that enhance its use as an assessment tool. It is compatible with the IPLM in that it can load configuration files created with the teaching microworld. It differs in that it does not allow users to view or configure the list of simulated faulty equipment, more correctly reflecting real-world situations where students must diagnose equipment as faulty using available troubleshooting tools.
requirements: Compatible with IPLM configuration files
constraints: Does not allow users to view or configure the list of simulated faulty equipment
target_learning_goals: Assessment of computer networking problem-solving skills
examples: Instructors prepared networks with incorrect IP settings, faulty cables, faulty network cards, faulty switch ports, and faulty switches or WAN modems for troubleshooting exercises

article_title: Comparing between face-to-face and mobile learning for improving nurses' performance in premature infant positioning: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Sabeti Fahimeh, Ranjbar Azadeh, Kashaki Mandana, Khanjari Sedigheh, Banazadeh Marjan. (2026). Comparing between face-to-face and mobile learning for improving nurses’ performance in premature infant positioning: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09855-8
title: Infant Positioning Assessment Tool (IPAT)
description: The IPAT, developed by Coughlin et al., is a dual-purpose instrument that "assesses infant positioning and acts as an educational resource, providing a visual reminder of essential positioning components." It scores six anatomical regions (head, chin/neck, shoulders, hands/arms, pelvis, knees/ankles/feet) from 0 to 2 each, yielding total scores from 0 to 12. Scores below 8 indicate a need for change, 8–10 acceptable, and 10–12 ideal. Inter-observer reliability was reported at 0.957.
requirements: Trained evaluator for consistent scoring application
constraints: Evaluator blinding to group allocation was not possible due to the inherent characteristics of the interventions
examples: Used at baseline, one week, and one month post-intervention with three observations per participant per timepoint

article_title: Interprofessional simulation training in acute pediatrics using rapid cycle deliberate practice (ip-star).
citation: Kumar Manish, Mittal Mahima, Chavan Seema Shankarsingh, Krishnan S Vimal, Gilbert John H.V., Sanatombi Devi Elsa. (2025). Interprofessional simulation training in acute pediatrics using rapid cycle deliberate practice (ip-star). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08302-4
title: IP-STAR: an instructional model integrating RCDP methodology within the TeamSTEPPS framework for interprofessional simulation
description: IP-STAR combines Rapid Cycle Deliberate Practice, in which learners "repetitiously perform a simulation scenario, segmented into progressively complex stages, with frequent and succinct micro-debriefs by faculty", with the TeamSTEPPS framework whose four core components — communication, leadership, situational monitoring and mutual support — are presented as teachable-learnable skills. The model was operationalized as a two-hour in-situ pediatric cardiac arrest simulation for mixed MBBS and nursing teams, with hard stops for objective-critical actions and soft stops for team-dynamics variability. The authors position this combination as previously largely unexplored for undergraduate interprofessional healthcare education.
requirements: Faculty trained in RCDP and TeamSTEPPS principles to deliver micro-debriefs and score TPOT; a validated scenario script (s-CVI 0.93) segmented into rounds with predetermined learning objectives
constraints: Evidence for RCDP for non-technical team skills was described as relatively sparse before this study
The study was a pilot in an institute with no formal IPE curriculum
target_learners: third-year undergraduate medical (MBBS) and BSc Nursing students
target_learning_goals: pediatric cardiac arrest management knowledge and skills
teamwork competencies including communication, leadership, situational monitoring and mutual support
examples: Twelve sessions each with 3–4 MBBS and 2–3 nursing students practicing a five-round pediatric cardiac arrest scenario, each iteration restarting from Round 1
key_sources: Kumar Manish, Mittal Mahima, Chavan Seema Shankarsingh, Krishnan S Vimal, Gilbert John H.V., Sanatombi Devi Elsa. (2025). Interprofessional simulation training in acute pediatrics using rapid cycle deliberate practice (ip-star). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08302-4

article_title: Interprofessional simulation training in acute pediatrics using rapid cycle deliberate practice (ip-star).
citation: Kumar Manish, Mittal Mahima, Chavan Seema Shankarsingh, Krishnan S Vimal, Gilbert John H.V., Sanatombi Devi Elsa. (2025). Interprofessional simulation training in acute pediatrics using rapid cycle deliberate practice (ip-star). BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08302-4
title: Five-round progressive RCDP scenario structure pairing technical objectives with TeamSTEPPS team-performance objectives
description: The IP-STAR scenario was segmented into five structured RCDP rounds, each with predetermined learning objectives: Round 1 recognition of arrest, calling for help, CPR initiation, role allocation and monitor attachment; Round 2 high-quality CPR and bag-mask ventilation; Round 3 epinephrine, rhythm checks and the PALS algorithm; Round 4 airway management and reversible causes; Round 5 post-resuscitation care and SBAR handover. Across all rounds, demonstration of TeamSTEPPS elements was the overarching objective, and each iteration recommenced from Round 1 to reinforce prior learning. Hard stops marked actions that must be performed in the recommended way; soft stops allowed performance variability.
requirements: Debrief guidance pre-decided as hard stops and soft stops; progression to the next round only once learners demonstrate reasonable proficiency
constraints: Each iteration commences from Round 1, so later-round content is practiced only within restarted sequences
target_learners: novice undergraduate medical and nursing learners
examples: Round 3 required prompt epinephrine administration, rhythm checks and following the PALS algorithm

title: IP-STAR in-situ low-technology simulation module for acute pediatric cardiac arrest team training
description: IP-STAR is a two-hour interprofessional simulation module using a low-technology PRESTAN® Infant Manikin coupled with enhanced environmental fidelity using hospital props such as standard pediatric ward equipment, hospital clothing, and crash cart trolleys. It was delivered in-situ within the clinical environment with simulation-safety practices including saline-filled vials labeled for simulation purposes only. The scenario, an 8-month-old infant in pulseless electrical activity with hypovolemic shock, was validated by five external experts with s-CVI 0.93 and referenced the six CIHC competency domains.
requirements: In-situ delivery must not affect routine patient care; simulation-safety practices such as decontamination of returned equipment
constraints: Biprofessional composition (medical and nursing only) constrains ecological validity relative to real emergency teams
target_learners: third-year MBBS and BSc Nursing students in interprofessional teams of 5–7
examples: Use of empty medication vials filled with saline and clearly labeled for simulation purposes only

article_title: Evidence-Based Suturing Education for Midwives.
citation: Yeager Amanda Love CNM, DNP; Nypaver Cynthia CNM, PhD, WHNP‐BC. (2025). Evidence‐Based Suturing Education for Midwives. Journal of Midwifery & Women's Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmwh.70018
title: Live-streamed expert demonstration on student iPads during the suturing workshop
description: A technology-supported demonstration setup in which a camera focused closely on the instructor's hands and the live feed was projected onto Apple iPads at each student's desk, set up by an educational technology expert. The article reports that "Bringing the demonstration directly to the student's desk successfully increased student‐faculty ratios, as more students could view the instructor's hands simultaneously despite being in a larger room." Students could also review previous videos, adjust playback speed, and record their own hands for later viewing.
requirements: An educational technology expert to set up the iPads and camera feed, plus iPads at each student desk
constraints: Institutional cost is dependent on the use of high‐fidelity or low‐fidelity models; supplies and technology entail significant financial investment
target_learning_goals: observing expert suturing technique with optimal visualization
examples: The physician demonstrated repair of a second-degree perineal laceration in real time at a high-top table while the live feed played on student iPads

BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07299-0
title: IPSE (Improving Psychological Security and Empowerment) model for nursing care of potential organ donors
description: The IPSE model is a nursing care model developed through qualitative studies to structure care of brain-dead patients who are candidates for organ donation. The article states it "covers all aspects of patient care, such as providing 'informational and educational support' and 'management support'". In this trial, both interventions' educational materials and gamification scenarios were organized around its dimensions: educational support (brain death definition and diagnostics), informational support (physiological monitoring of organ-eligible patients), and management support (legal aspects and family communication).
requirements: Educational materials and scenarios must be designed around the model's dimensions of educational, informational, and management support
constraints: Developed for the specific context of caring for brain-dead patients who are candidates for organ donation
target_learners: ICU nurses caring for brain-dead patients and organ donation candidates
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of brain death diagnosis and donor care
Communication with patients' families and legal aspects of donation
examples: Two two-hour webinars and six gamified scenarios were structured on the IPSE model's dimensions

title: Six-scenario gamification training with points and progression gating delivered via messaging platform
description: An email- and messaging-platform-based gamification intervention in which nurses "received an email containing a link to 6 scenarios, each with 4 questions". Each correct first-attempt answer earned one point; correct answers were shown immediately; progression to the next scenario required answering all questions correctly; nurses scoring below 70% had to review materials and retry. Scenarios mapped to IPSE model dimensions, from brain death understanding through family communication, and the intervention lasted one month.
requirements: Nurses must study the educational materials before receiving scenario links
Progression gating requires answering all questions in a scenario correctly; below 70% triggers retry

target_learners: ICU nurses in hospitals affiliated with medical universities in Iran
